The President is meant to stand above party politics and represent the whole country – which is why many presidents suspend their party membership during their term.
87.otherOptions: The Federal Chancellor is the head of government, not the head of state. The President of the Bundestag chairs parliament. The President of the Bundesrat is a trap: they deputise for the Federal President when the latter is unable to act (Article 57) – but that does not make them head of state.
87.memoryTip: Head of state = Federal President; head of government = Federal Chancellor.

88.summary: The parliamentary opposition scrutinises the government.
88.whyCorrect: It asks critical questions, makes counter-proposals and can set up committees of inquiry.
88.background: The opposition consists of all parliamentary groups in the Bundestag that are not part of the government. It has an important scrutiny role: in debates, question time and written questions, it challenges the government to explain its policies. Just one quarter of the members can demand a committee of inquiry (Article 44) or have a law reviewed by the Federal Constitutional Court. The opposition is also a possible government of tomorrow.
88.otherOptions: The Federal Chancellor decides who becomes a federal minister. The state governments decide who sits in the Bundesrat. The heads of the state governments are elected by the state parliaments. The opposition in the Bundestag has no influence on any of this.
88.memoryTip: The government governs – the opposition scrutinises.

89.summary: The association of a party’s members in parliament is called a parliamentary group (Fraktion).
89.whyCorrect: In the Bundestag, a parliamentary group needs at least five percent of the members.
89.background: Members of the same party join together in parliament to form a Fraktion. The group discusses its positions together, divides the work in the committees and decides who speaks in the plenary. Parliamentary groups have special rights, for example speaking time, committee seats and funding for their work. The CDU and CSU form a joint parliamentary group in the Bundestag.
89.otherOptions: An association (Verband) represents interests outside parliament, such as a business or welfare association. The Council of Elders (Ältestenrat) is a body that helps the President of the Bundestag organise parliamentary work. The opposition is all groups that are not in government.

90.summary: The federal states take part in federal legislation through the Bundesrat.
90.whyCorrect: Article 50 of the Basic Law: “The states shall participate through the Bundesrat in the legislation and administration of the federation.”
90.background: After being passed by the Bundestag, every federal law goes to the Bundesrat. For laws requiring consent – for example when the states have to implement a law or spend money on it – the law cannot enter into force without the Bundesrat. For other laws, the Bundesrat can raise an objection, which the Bundestag can override. In case of disagreement, the mediation committee can seek a compromise.
90.otherOptions: The Federal Convention only elects the Federal President. The Bundestag is made up of elected federal members of parliament, not representatives of the states. The federal government is the government of the federation.
90.memoryTip: States → Bundesrat → a say in federal laws.

91.summary: Governing at federal level becomes more difficult if a change of government in a state changes the majority in the Bundesrat.
91.whyCorrect: The state governments sit in the Bundesrat; if a state government changes, the votes in the Bundesrat change too.
91.background: For many federal laws, the federal government also needs a majority in the Bundesrat – at least 35 of the 69 votes. If, after a state election, a party that is in opposition at federal level joins the state government, the federal government can lose this majority. It then has to negotiate with the states and make compromises. That is why state elections are watched closely across the country.
91.otherOptions: The majority in the Bundestag does not change through a state election – the Bundestag is only elected in the federal election. New parties in the Bundesrat do not automatically make governing easier, and whether a state is rich or poor plays no role in its Bundesrat votes.
91.memoryTip: State election → state government → Bundesrat → federal politics.

92.summary: CSU stands for Christian Social Union (Christlich-Soziale Union).
92.whyCorrect: The CSU is the CDU’s sister party and runs only in Bavaria.
92.background: The Christian Social Union (CSU) was founded in Bavaria in 1945. It runs in elections only in Bavaria, and in return the CDU does not run there. In the Bundestag, the CDU and CSU form a joint parliamentary group, the “Union”. For decades the CSU has almost always provided the Bavarian Minister-President, since 2018 Markus Söder.
92.otherOptions: “Christian Safe Union” and “Christian South German Union” are invented names – even though the CSU really is a southern German party. A “Christian Social Business Association” is not a party.
92.memoryTip: CSU = Christian Social Union – the S stands for “Social”.

93.summary: The more second votes a party receives, the more seats it gets in parliament.
93.whyCorrect: The second vote determines the distribution of seats in the Bundestag.
93.background: In the federal election, every voter has two votes. With the first vote you choose a person in your constituency, with the second vote a party. The second votes determine how many of the 630 seats each party receives (proportional representation). A party usually needs at least five percent of the second votes for this. Since the 2023 electoral reform, constituency winners only receive a seat if it is covered by their party’s second votes.
93.otherOptions: First and second votes are independent of each other; many second votes do not mean fewer first votes. How many constituency candidates enter parliament depends on the first votes in the constituencies. And more second votes actually make it less likely that a party has to form a coalition.
93.memoryTip: Second vote = the more important vote: it decides the seats.

94.summary: You can vote in the Bundestag election from the age of 18.
94.whyCorrect: The Basic Law sets the voting age for the Bundestag at 18 (Article 38).
94.background: Eligible to vote in the federal election are German citizens who are at least 18 years old and have lived in Germany for at least three months (or meet certain conditions as Germans abroad). Other elections partly have different rules: since 2024, people in Germany can vote in the European election from 16, and in several federal states also in local or state elections.
94.otherOptions: 16 applies in Germany for the European election and some elections in the states, but not for the federal election. 21 and 23 are too high; a voting age of 21 applied in the Federal Republic until 1970.

95.summary: Compulsory schooling applies to most children in Germany.
95.whyCorrect: Children in Germany must attend school; home schooling is generally not allowed.
95.background: Compulsory schooling usually starts at the age of six and lasts nine or ten years of full-time school, depending on the federal state; after that, there is often an obligation to attend vocational school. It is regulated in the states’ school laws. Compulsory schooling applies to all children living in Germany, regardless of their nationality. Parents who do not send their children to school can be fined.
95.otherOptions: Germany has no compulsory voting, and children cannot vote anyway. Confidentiality obligations apply, for example, to doctors, lawyers or priests towards other people. There is no religious obligation because of freedom of religion.

96.summary: Denying the Holocaust can be punished with imprisonment of up to five years or a fine.
96.whyCorrect: This is set out in Section 130 of the Criminal Code (incitement to hatred).
96.background: In the Holocaust, the National Socialists murdered around six million Jews from all over Europe. Anyone in Germany who publicly or in an assembly denies, approves of or trivialises this genocide commits a criminal offence if it is capable of disturbing public peace. The Criminal Code provides for imprisonment of up to five years or a fine. This is where freedom of expression ends, because the dignity of the victims and public peace are protected.
96.otherOptions: Cutting social benefits or community service hours are not penalties the law provides for Holocaust denial. And Holocaust denial is not allowed – it is a criminal offence.
96.memoryTip: Denying the Holocaust = a crime (Section 130 StGB): up to five years in prison.

97.summary: Anyone in permanent employment automatically pays social insurance contributions.
97.whyCorrect: The employer deducts the contributions from the wage and pays them directly to social insurance.
97.background: With permanent employment, employees are usually compulsorily insured in health, long-term care, pension and unemployment insurance. You do not have to transfer the contributions yourself: the employer deducts them from your gross pay, adds its own share and pays everything to the health insurance fund, which passes it on. Your payslip shows the contributions exactly. The employer also deducts income tax.
97.otherOptions: Social assistance, child benefit and housing benefit are benefits you receive from the state if you meet certain conditions – you do not pay them.
97.memoryTip: Employed = social insurance is deducted automatically.

98.summary: If members of the Bundestag change parliamentary groups, the government can lose its majority.
98.whyCorrect: Members keep their seat; if the government has only a narrow majority, a few switches can cost it.
98.background: According to Article 38 of the Basic Law, members of parliament are “representatives of the whole people, not bound by orders or instructions and responsible only to their conscience”. This is called the free mandate. That is why they may change their parliamentary group or party and still remain in the Bundestag. If members switch from a governing group to the opposition, the coalition can lose its majority – and with it, struggle to pass laws.
98.otherOptions: Members may continue to attend sessions after changing groups. The Federal President does not have to agree. And voters do not get to vote again – the seat remains until the next election.
98.memoryTip: Free mandate: the seat belongs to the member, not the party.

99.summary: Social insurance is paid for jointly by employers and employees.
99.whyCorrect: In most branches, the contributions are split roughly half and half.
99.background: Health, long-term care, pension and unemployment insurance are usually financed in roughly equal parts by employees and employers. There are a few special features: statutory accident insurance is paid by employers alone, and health and long-term care insurance include additional contributions or surcharges, for example for people without children. The state also adds money from taxes, especially for pension insurance.
99.otherOptions: Only employees or only employers – both are wrong, because the costs are shared. “All citizens” is also wrong: contributions are paid by those in employment subject to social insurance, regardless of nationality.
99.memoryTip: Social insurance = split half and half between employer and employee.

100.summary: Life insurance is not part of statutory social insurance.
100.whyCorrect: Life insurance is a voluntary private insurance.
100.background: Statutory social insurance has five branches: health, long-term care, pension, unemployment and accident insurance. It is compulsory for most employees and financed through contributions from employees and employers. Life insurance, on the other hand, is taken out voluntarily with a private insurance company, for example to protect relatives in case of death or to save for old age.
100.otherOptions: Statutory pension insurance, unemployment insurance and long-term care insurance are all part of statutory social insurance.
100.memoryTip: “Statutory” = compulsory and organised by the state; life insurance = private and voluntary.

101.summary: Trade unions are interest groups of employees.
101.whyCorrect: They represent the interests of workers, for example regarding wages and working hours.
101.background: Article 9(3) of the Basic Law guarantees the right to form associations to safeguard and improve working and economic conditions – freedom of association. Trade unions negotiate collective agreements with employers’ associations on wages, holidays and working hours. If negotiations fail, they can call a strike. Well-known unions are IG Metall and ver.di; many are united in the German Trade Union Confederation (DGB).
101.otherOptions: Employers have their own interest groups, the employers’ associations – they are the unions’ negotiating partners. There are youth organisations for young people and social and senior citizens’ associations for pensioners, but these are not trade unions.
101.memoryTip: Trade union = for employees; employers’ association = for employers.

102.summary: Outstanding achievements can be honoured with the Federal Cross of Merit (Bundesverdienstkreuz).
102.whyCorrect: The Federal Cross of Merit is the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany and is awarded by the Federal President.
102.background: The Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany, usually called the Federal Cross of Merit, was established in 1951 by Federal President Theodor Heuss. It is the federation’s only general award for services to the common good – in politics, business, culture, science, sport or in social and voluntary work. Anyone can nominate a person; it is awarded by the Federal President.
102.otherOptions: The federal eagle is the heraldic animal, not an award. The “Patriotic Order of Merit” and the honorary title “Hero of the German Democratic Republic” were awards of the GDR, which no longer exist since 1990.

103.summary: A “traffic light coalition” is a government of the SPD, FDP and Alliance 90/The Greens.
103.whyCorrect: The name comes from the party colours red (SPD), yellow (FDP) and green (Greens) – like a traffic light.
103.background: In Germany, coalitions are often named after the parties’ colours: black stands for the CDU/CSU, red for the SPD, yellow for the FDP and green for the Greens. From 2021 to 2024, a traffic light coalition under Federal Chancellor Olaf Scholz governed at federal level; it collapsed in November 2024. Other well-known names are “grand coalition” (CDU/CSU and SPD) and “Jamaica” (black, yellow, green – the colours of the Jamaican flag).
103.otherOptions: The CDU and CSU form a joint parliamentary group in the Bundestag, the “Union” – that is not a coalition in the usual sense. The CDU/CSU and SPD together are called a “grand coalition” or “black-red”. A coalition of the CSU, the Left and the Greens has never existed.
103.memoryTip: Traffic light = red, yellow, green = SPD, FDP, Greens.

104.summary: Pregnancy must not be a reason for dismissal if the boss knows about it.
104.whyCorrect: The Maternity Protection Act prohibits dismissal during pregnancy and up to four months after giving birth.
104.background: Pregnant women and young mothers are specially protected in Germany. Under the Maternity Protection Act, an employer may generally not dismiss a woman during pregnancy and up to four months after childbirth if the employer knows about the pregnancy or is informed of it shortly after the dismissal. There is also special protection against dismissal during parental leave. In addition, the General Equal Treatment Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of sex.
104.otherOptions: Long illness, frequent lateness or doing private things during working hours can justify dismissal under certain conditions – in the case of misconduct, usually only after a formal warning. Pregnancy, however, is not misconduct and must not be a reason for dismissal.
104.memoryTip: Pregnant = special protection against dismissal (maternity protection).

105.summary: Election workers count the votes after the polls close.
105.whyCorrect: At the polling station they form the electoral board, which runs the election and counts the votes in public.
105.background: On election day, volunteer election workers work in every polling station. They check whether someone is on the electoral roll, hand out ballot papers and make sure the vote is secret. Polling stations close at 6 pm; then the election workers count the votes. The count is public – anyone may watch. They report the results to the election office. Workers usually receive a small allowance for their work.
105.otherOptions: Everyone votes alone in the polling booth; anyone who needs help can bring a helper of their choice – that is not a general task of election workers. The municipality sends out polling cards by post beforehand. Election workers may not pass interim results to the media.

106.summary: Volunteer election workers count the votes after the polls close.
106.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 105, just with different answers.
106.background: Elections in Germany are largely organised by citizens who help voluntarily. In a federal election, several hundred thousand people take part. Municipalities often recruit election workers among their staff or call for volunteers publicly; in principle, people can also be required to serve. This is democracy in action: citizens themselves check that the votes are counted correctly.
106.otherOptions: Children cannot vote, and election workers do not generally help older people in the polling booth. The municipality sends out the cards and letters stating the polling station (the polling card). Passing interim results to journalists is not one of their tasks.
106.memoryTip: Election workers = count the votes (as in question 105).

107.summary: The Bundestag is elected for four years.
107.whyCorrect: Article 39 of the Basic Law sets the legislative term at four years.
107.background: The Bundestag’s legislative term lasts four years. It begins with the first session of the new Bundestag and ends with the first session of the next one. Only in exceptional cases is there an early election, for example when the Federal Chancellor asks for a vote of confidence, loses it and the Federal President dissolves the Bundestag – as happened most recently in December 2024 before the election in February 2025.
107.otherOptions: Two, six or eight years are wrong. Most state parliaments and the European Parliament are elected for five years, as is the Federal President – only the Bundestag is elected for four.
107.memoryTip: Bundestag: 4 years. State parliament, European Parliament, Federal President: 5 years.

108.summary: Anyone who is a German citizen and at least 18 years old may vote in the federal election.
108.whyCorrect: German citizens aged 18 and over are eligible to vote (Article 38 of the Basic Law, Federal Electoral Act).
108.background: The right to vote in Bundestag elections depends on German citizenship. That is why naturalisation is so important for political participation: only with a German passport can you vote for the Bundestag and the state parliaments. You must also be 18 and usually have lived in Germany for at least three months. Germans living abroad can also vote under certain conditions.
108.otherOptions: Living in Germany is not enough: foreign nationals cannot vote in the Bundestag election; EU citizens can, however, vote in local and European elections. “Three years in Germany” is not a requirement, and the voting age is 18, not 21.

109.summary: Federal elections normally take place every four years.
109.whyCorrect: The Bundestag’s legislative term lasts four years (Article 39).
109.background: The Bundestag is regularly re-elected every four years. The election always takes place on a Sunday or public holiday so that as many people as possible have time. Anyone unable to vote on election day can vote in advance by post. Only if the Bundestag is dissolved early does the election take place sooner – this has happened four times so far in the history of the Federal Republic (1972, 1983, 2005 and 2025).
109.otherOptions: Every three, five or six years is wrong. Five years applies to most state parliaments, the European Parliament and the Federal President’s term.

110.summary: The Bundestag is elected for four years.
110.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 107, just with different answer options.
110.background: Four years is a compromise: long enough for a government to implement its plans, and short enough for voters to decide regularly whether they are satisfied with its policies. Legislative terms in many other countries are of similar length, for example five years in Austria or two years for the US House of Representatives.
110.otherOptions: Two and three years are too short; five years applies to most state parliaments and the European Parliament, not the Bundestag.
110.memoryTip: Questions 107 and 110: the answer is always 4 years.

111.summary: Publicly calling for the destruction of Israel is forbidden in Germany.
111.whyCorrect: It can be punished as incitement to hatred or as public incitement to commit crimes.
111.background: Because of the Holocaust, Germany bears a special historical responsibility towards Jews and the State of Israel. German governments describe Israel’s security as part of Germany’s “reason of state”. Anyone who publicly calls for the destruction of Israel is calling for violence and genocide. This is not covered by freedom of expression and can be punished under the Criminal Code. Publicly burning foreign flags has also been a criminal offence since 2020.
111.otherOptions: You may publicly criticise and discuss Israel’s policies – this is protected by freedom of expression, as with any other state. Hanging an Israeli flag on your own property is of course allowed.
111.memoryTip: Criticising policy – allowed. Calling for destruction – forbidden.

112.whyCorrect: Nobody may find out whom a person voted for (Article 38 of the Basic Law).
112.background: Secret is one of the five electoral principles: general, direct, free, equal and secret. That is why you mark your ballot alone in a polling booth and fold it before putting it in the ballot box. Postal voters must also declare that they filled in the ballot personally and unobserved. The secret ballot protects people from being put under pressure because of their vote.
112.otherOptions: “Special”, “job-related” and “gender-dependent” are not electoral principles. On the contrary: elections are general and equal – job and gender play no role.

113.summary: An election in Germany is won by the party that receives the most votes.
113.whyCorrect: In the federal election, the second votes are decisive for this.
113.background: The party with the most votes is the winner of the election and receives the most seats in parliament. But who then governs is only decided in coalition negotiations: the government needs a majority of the seats. Usually the strongest party leads the government – but a coalition without it can also be formed, such as the SPD–FDP coalition under Willy Brandt in 1969.
113.otherOptions: All votes count equally, whether they come from men, women, workers or other groups. You cannot vote directly for a chancellor candidate: with the first vote you choose a person in your constituency, and the Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag.
113.memoryTip: Most votes = winner. All votes count equally.

114.summary: Taking part in democratic elections in Germany is a right.
114.whyCorrect: There is no compulsory voting; everyone can decide for themselves whether to vote.
114.background: The right to vote is one of the most important political rights: through their vote, citizens decide who represents them in parliament. In Germany, participation is voluntary – a free election also includes the freedom not to vote. Nevertheless, politicians and society encourage people to vote, because high turnout strengthens democracy. In the 2025 federal election it was over 82 percent.
114.otherOptions: There is no duty or compulsion to vote in Germany – unlike, for example, in Belgium or Australia. Voting is not a “burden” either; it is an opportunity to have a say.
114.memoryTip: Voting is a right, not a duty.

115.summary: “Active voting right” means: you can vote.
115.whyCorrect: Anyone with the active right to vote may cast their vote in an election.
115.background: There are two sides to the right to vote. The active right to vote is the right to vote – to cast your vote. The passive right to vote is the right to be elected – to stand as a candidate. For the Bundestag, German citizens aged 18 and over have both rights.
115.otherOptions: “You can be elected” describes the passive right to vote. You do not have to vote in Germany – there is no compulsory voting. And nobody has to go to the vote count; it is public, so you are allowed to watch.
115.memoryTip: Active = voting yourself. Passive = being elected.

116.summary: If you are allowed to vote in a federal election, you have the active right to vote.
116.whyCorrect: The active right to vote is the right to cast your vote in an election.
116.background: This question is closely linked to question 115. German citizens aged 18 and over have the active right to vote for the Bundestag. With naturalisation you gain this right – and also the passive right to vote, i.e. the possibility of standing for a parliament yourself.
116.otherOptions: An election campaign is the parties’ advertising before an election, with posters, speeches and debates. The electoral procedure is the way the election is run. None of these terms describes the right to vote.
116.memoryTip: Being allowed to vote = active right to vote.

117.summary: Parties need at least 5 percent of the second votes to enter the Bundestag.
117.whyCorrect: This is the so-called 5 percent threshold.
117.background: The 5 percent threshold is meant to prevent a very large number of small parties from sitting in parliament and making it difficult to form a government – a lesson from the Weimar Republic. There are exceptions: a party that directly wins at least three constituencies also enters the Bundestag. Parties of national minorities, such as the SSW of the Danish minority, are exempt from the threshold.
117.otherOptions: 3, 4 or 6 percent are wrong. In 2025, for example, the FDP and BSW fell just short of 5 percent and are therefore not in the Bundestag.
117.memoryTip: Five percent – like the five fingers of a hand.

118.summary: Anyone can become a member of the Jewish Maccabi sports clubs.
118.whyCorrect: Maccabi clubs are open to everyone – regardless of religion, origin or nationality.
118.background: Makkabi Deutschland is the umbrella organisation of Jewish gymnastics and sports clubs in Germany, with around 40 local clubs. Jewish sports clubs already existed before 1933; under National Socialism they were banned. Makkabi Deutschland was re-founded in 1965. Today many members are not Jewish – the clubs see themselves as open places of encounter and campaign against antisemitism and racism in sport.
118.otherOptions: Maccabi clubs are not only for Germans, not only for Israelis and not only for religious people. As in any sports club, anyone who enjoys sport and community can take part.

119.summary: A free election means: everyone can decide without coercion whether to vote and whom to vote for.
119.whyCorrect: Nobody may put voters under pressure or force them to vote in a certain way.
119.background: Freedom of election is one of the five electoral principles in the Basic Law (Article 38). It protects against pressure from the state, employers, family or other people. Free also means: you may spoil your ballot or not vote at all. This question is closely related to question 5.
119.otherOptions: Convicted offenders can usually vote; only in rare cases can a court take away the right to vote. Since elections take place on Sundays, you usually do not need time off from your employer. And you cannot freely choose your polling station – it depends on where you live; with a polling certificate, however, you can vote by post or at another polling station in your constituency.
119.memoryTip: Free = without coercion – whether and whom.

120.summary: Germany’s electoral system combines majority voting and proportional representation.
120.whyCorrect: With the first vote a constituency candidate is elected by majority, with the second vote a party by proportional representation.
120.background: The German system is called personalised proportional representation. The second votes determine how many seats each party receives in the Bundestag – that is the proportional part. With the first vote, voters choose a person in each of the 299 constituencies; whoever gets the most votes wins the constituency – that is the majority part. This way each region has its own members of parliament, while the distribution of seats still reflects the parties’ share of the vote.
120.otherOptions: Under a census suffrage, the right to vote depends on property or taxes; under the three-class franchise (in Prussia until 1918), the rich had more weight. A men-only suffrage no longer exists: women in Germany have been able to vote since 1918.
120.memoryTip: First vote = majority (person), second vote = proportional (party).

121.summary: The minimum share of votes a party needs for the Bundestag is called the 5 percent threshold.
121.whyCorrect: A party must receive at least five percent of the second votes.
121.background: The 5 percent threshold applies to the federal election and most state elections. It is intended to prevent parliament from splitting into many small groups, as happened in the Weimar Republic. Critics say that many votes are “lost” as a result. However, the Federal Constitutional Court considers the threshold permissible for the Bundestag because it makes stable governments possible. There is currently no threshold for the European election in Germany.
121.otherOptions: “Admission limit”, “base value” and “directive” are not technical terms for this rule. A directive, for example, is a legal act of the EU.

122.summary: Elections in Germany are free, equal and secret.
122.whyCorrect: Add to this “general” and “direct” – together, the five electoral principles from Article 38.
122.background: The five electoral principles are: general (all eligible voters may vote), direct (the vote goes directly to candidates or parties, without electors), free (without pressure or coercion), equal (every vote counts the same) and secret (nobody finds out whom you voted for). This answer names three of them.
122.otherOptions: “Open” contradicts the principle of the secret ballot. “Closed” and “safe” are not electoral principles, and “voluntary” is not stated as such in the Basic Law – even though there is no compulsory voting.

123.summary: The 5 percent threshold is the minimum share of votes a party needs to enter parliament.
123.whyCorrect: In the federal election this means five percent of the second votes.
123.background: A party that receives less than five percent of the second votes generally gets no seats in the Bundestag. Its votes are not taken into account when seats are allocated. Exceptions apply to parties that directly win at least three constituencies and to parties of national minorities. Questions 117 and 121 deal with the same rule.
123.otherOptions: The 5 percent threshold has nothing to do with votes in the Bundestag or Bundesrat and is not an attendance check. It applies at the election, not afterwards in parliament.
123.memoryTip: 5 percent threshold = the entry ticket to parliament.

124.summary: The federal election is the election of the parliament for Germany.
124.whyCorrect: In the federal election, citizens elect the members of the German Bundestag.
124.background: The Bundestag is the parliament of the Federal Republic. In the federal election, its members are elected for four years; since 2025 there have been 630 of them. The newly elected Bundestag then elects the Federal Chancellor. Many people already have the chancellor candidate in mind when they vote – but the ballot only lists constituency candidates and parties.
124.otherOptions: The Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag, the Federal President by the Federal Convention. The state parliaments are elected in state elections.
124.memoryTip: Federal election = election of the Bundestag (parliament).

125.summary: Regular elections make it possible to change the government according to the will of the majority of voters.
125.whyCorrect: If the majority is dissatisfied with the government, it can elect a different one at the next election.
125.background: In a democracy, power is only granted for a limited time. Through regular elections, citizens can confirm or vote out the government – peacefully and without violence. This forces politicians to seek people’s approval and to be accountable. Germany has seen many such peaceful changes of power since 1949.
125.otherOptions: Elections do not force anyone to vote – there is no compulsory voting. They are not meant to preserve existing laws, but precisely to make change possible. And elections do not give any particular group more power: every vote counts the same, whether poor or rich.
125.memoryTip: Election = a peaceful change of government is possible.

126.summary: Before an election, eligible voters receive a polling card (Wahlbenachrichtigung) from their municipality.
126.whyCorrect: The municipality sends it by post no later than three weeks before the election to everyone on the electoral roll.
126.background: The polling card shows the election date, the opening hours and the polling station where you can vote. On the back there is usually an application for postal voting. You bring the polling card and an ID document to the polling station. Anyone who is eligible but has not received a card should contact the municipality in good time and check whether they are on the electoral roll.
126.otherOptions: There is no “voting permit” from the Federal President – the right to vote comes from the law. The Federal Convention only elects the Federal President and does not write to voters. A parish office belongs to the church and has nothing to do with elections.
126.memoryTip: Letter from the municipality = polling card.

127.summary: The 5 percent threshold exists because many small parties make it harder to form a government.
127.whyCorrect: It is meant to prevent a fragmented parliament and make stable majorities possible.
127.background: In the Weimar Republic, more than a dozen parties sat in the Reichstag at times. Finding stable majorities was very difficult and governments changed often – this contributed to the failure of democracy. The authors of the Basic Law and the electoral laws wanted to prevent this. That is why a party needs at least five percent of the second votes in the federal election to receive seats.
127.otherOptions: Whether small parties have similar programmes plays no role in the rule. Citizens’ orientation is not the reason – many parties can still appear on the ballot. And politicians are not paid by their parties: members of parliament receive an allowance from public funds.
127.memoryTip: Fewer splinter parties → easier to form a government.

128.summary: Members of parliament elected by citizens are called Abgeordnete (members of parliament).
128.whyCorrect: They represent citizens in the Bundestag, a state parliament or the European Parliament.
128.background: Members of parliament are elected by the people and are “representatives of the whole people” (Article 38 of the Basic Law). They debate and pass laws, scrutinise the government and take care of the concerns of people in their constituency. Since 2025 there have been 630 members of the Bundestag. They receive an allowance for their work.
128.otherOptions: The Federal Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag, not directly by citizens. Ambassadors represent Germany abroad and are appointed, not elected. Minister-Presidents are elected by the state parliaments.
128.memoryTip: Sent to parliament by the people = members of parliament.

129.summary: In Germany, the Bundestag is elected by the people.
129.whyCorrect: The Chancellor, Minister-Presidents and Federal President, by contrast, are elected indirectly.
129.background: Germany is a representative democracy: the people directly elect the parliaments – the Bundestag, the state parliaments, the municipal councils and the European Parliament. The parliaments then elect other offices. The Bundestag elects the Federal Chancellor, the state parliaments elect the Minister-Presidents, and the Federal Convention elects the Federal President. At local level, citizens in most states also elect the mayor directly.
129.otherOptions: The Federal Chancellor, Minister-Presidents and Federal President are not elected directly by the people. This is deliberate: the Basic Law relies on strong parliaments.
129.memoryTip: The people elect parliaments; parliaments elect the heads of government.

130.whyCorrect: It has exactly one cross in the first-vote column and exactly one in the second-vote column.
130.background: In the federal election you have two votes. On the left, you use the first vote to mark a person from your constituency; on the right, you use the second vote to mark a party. There may be at most one cross in each column. You do not have to cast both votes – then only the one you cast counts. A vote becomes invalid if there are several crosses in one column, if you write something extra or if your intention is unclear.
130.otherOptions: Ballots 2, 3 and 4 have several crosses in at least one column. Then it is not clear whom you want to vote for, and that vote is invalid.

131.summary: A mayor (Bürgermeister) is the head of a municipality.
131.whyCorrect: The mayor leads the municipal administration and represents the municipality externally.
131.background: Every town and municipality has a mayor; in larger cities the office is often called Lord Mayor (Oberbürgermeister). In most federal states the mayor is elected directly by the citizens. The mayor runs the administration in the town hall, implements the decisions of the municipal council and is the point of contact for local people.
131.otherOptions: A school is headed by a head teacher, a bank by a board of directors. A party is chaired by its party leader. The word “Bürgermeister” literally means the “master” of a municipality’s citizens.
131.memoryTip: Mayor = head of the municipality, works in the town hall.

132.summary: Volunteering (Ehrenamt) means working voluntarily and unpaid, for example in clubs and associations.
132.whyCorrect: Volunteers commit themselves to others in their free time without receiving a salary.
132.background: Volunteering is very common in Germany: around 40 percent of people aged 14 and over volunteer. They coach children in sports clubs, help in the volunteer fire brigade or the Federal Agency for Technical Relief, hand out food at food banks, support refugees or serve as election workers and lay judges. Many services would not work without this commitment. Some volunteer roles come with a small expense allowance.
132.otherOptions: Soldiers work professionally in the Bundeswehr and are paid. Anyone who works in the federal government or a hospital and earns money is working professionally, not as a volunteer.

133.summary: In federal and state elections you can vote by post.
133.whyCorrect: Anyone who cannot or does not want to go to the polling station on election day can vote by post in advance.
133.background: You apply for a postal vote at your municipality, for example using the form on the polling card or online. You then receive a polling certificate, the ballot paper and envelopes. You fill in the ballot personally and unobserved and send everything so that it arrives by 6 pm on election day at the latest. In the 2021 federal election, almost half of all voters voted by post.
133.otherOptions: Nobody may vote for someone else – not even a husband for his wife. This violates the principle of secret and personal voting and is a criminal offence. You cannot vote by phone. The voting age for the Bundestag and most state parliaments is 18; some states allow voting in state elections from 16, but not from 14.
133.memoryTip: Postal vote yes – proxies, phone and children no.

134.summary: To keep the bus line, you can join a citizens’ initiative or start one yourself.
134.whyCorrect: Citizens’ initiatives are a typical way to campaign locally for a shared concern.
134.background: In a citizens’ initiative, people with a common goal join together – for example to keep a bus line, a playground or a swimming pool. They collect signatures, talk to politicians on the municipal council, write to the press or organise demonstrations. In many states, a citizens’ petition can also lead to a local referendum on the issue. This is how democracy works between elections too.
134.otherOptions: A sports club and cycling training do not change the decision about the bus line. The tax office collects taxes and is not responsible for bus lines; being a taxpayer does not give you a right to a particular bus line. The forestry office looks after the forest.

135.whyCorrect: They campaign for better wages and working conditions for workers.
135.background: Trade unions are voluntary associations of workers. They negotiate collective agreements, advise their members on problems at work and provide legal protection, for example in the case of dismissal. In many companies they work together with works councils. Any employee can become a member; the fee is usually around one percent of gross pay. This question is closely related to question 101.
135.otherOptions: Large and small companies are represented by employers’ and business associations, such as chambers of industry and commerce. The self-employed have their own professional associations and chambers.
135.memoryTip: Trade union = the voice of employees.

136.summary: You go to the labour court, for example, in case of unjustified dismissal by your boss.
136.whyCorrect: Labour courts decide disputes between employees and employers.
136.background: Germany has special courts for conflicts arising from employment: the labour courts. They deal with dismissals, unpaid wages, holidays, references or formal warnings. At first instance you do not need a lawyer, and each side bears its own legal costs. Proceedings often begin with a conciliation hearing in which the court tries to reach an agreement.
136.otherOptions: An incorrect utility bill is a tenancy dispute – the local court (Amtsgericht) is responsible. Disputes with neighbours also go to the local court; often you must first try mediation. After a traffic accident, the issue is compensation (civil court) or a criminal offence (criminal court).

137.summary: The labour court is responsible for conflicts in the world of work.
137.whyCorrect: Labour courts are specialised courts for disputes arising from employment.
137.background: Labour jurisdiction has three levels: the labour court, the state labour court and the Federal Labour Court in Erfurt. Alongside professional judges, lay judges from both the employee and employer side take part in decisions. This brings practical experience into the judgments. Disputes between trade unions and employers, for example about strikes, also end up in the labour courts.
137.otherOptions: The family court decides on divorce, custody or maintenance. The criminal court hears criminal cases. The local court is responsible for many general civil and criminal matters, but not for labour law.
137.memoryTip: World of work → labour court → state labour court → Federal Labour Court.

138.summary: In case of unjustified dismissal, you can file an unfair dismissal claim (Kündigungsschutzklage).
138.whyCorrect: The claim must reach the labour court within three weeks of receiving the written notice of dismissal.
138.background: The Protection Against Dismissal Act protects employees from socially unjustified dismissal if they have worked at the company for more than six months and the company has more than ten employees. Anyone who considers the dismissal invalid must act quickly: after three weeks, the dismissal is otherwise deemed valid. Help is available from a lawyer, the trade union or the labour court’s legal application office. Such proceedings often end in a settlement, such as a severance payment.
138.otherOptions: Simply continuing to work and being friendly does not change the dismissal. A dunning procedure is intended for outstanding money claims, not for a dismissal. An unjustified dismissal is not a crime – the police are not responsible.
138.memoryTip: Dismissal → three weeks → unfair dismissal claim.

139.summary: A court trial takes place, for example, when someone has committed a crime and is charged.
139.whyCorrect: The public prosecutor brings charges, and a court decides on guilt and punishment in a main hearing.
139.background: When the police investigate a crime, the public prosecutor’s office checks whether there is enough evidence. It then brings charges, and a criminal trial follows. Until the verdict, the presumption of innocence applies: nobody is considered guilty until a court has established it. Every defendant has the right to a defence lawyer and to be heard in court (Article 103 of the Basic Law). Courts also decide disputes between citizens, for example about contracts or rent.
139.otherOptions: Changing your religion and holding a different opinion from the government are fundamental rights – you do not go to court for that. Wrong parking is an administrative offence: you get a fine and must pay for the towing. It only goes to court if you file an objection yourself.

140.summary: A lay judge (Schöffe) decides on guilt and punishment together with professional judges.
140.whyCorrect: Lay judges serve voluntarily in criminal proceedings and have the same vote as professional judges.
140.background: Lay judges are citizens without legal training who take part in decisions at criminal courts. This brings the perspective of the population into the administration of justice. They are elected for five years; the municipalities draw up lists of nominees. To become a lay judge, you must have German citizenship and be between 25 and 69 years old. There is compensation for loss of earnings.
140.otherOptions: Legal advice is given by lawyers. Documents are issued by authorities or notaries. The defendant is defended by a defence lawyer.
140.memoryTip: Lay judge = a citizen acting as a judge (voluntarily).

141.summary: A lawyer advises people on legal questions and represents them in court.
141.whyCorrect: Lawyers are independent advisers who represent their clients’ interests.
141.background: Lawyers have studied law and are admitted to the bar. They advise, for example, on tenancy agreements, problems at work, residence issues or a divorce and represent their clients in court. People with little money can apply for advice assistance or legal aid so that the state covers all or part of the costs. Consumer advice centres, tenants’ associations or trade unions also offer legal advice to their members.
141.otherOptions: Judges decide neutrally and may not represent either side. Lay judges are volunteer judges. Public prosecutors investigate and prosecute crimes – they represent the state, not individual citizens.
141.memoryTip: Lawyer = my representative; judge = neutral; prosecutor = accuser.

142.summary: A judge works at a court and delivers judgments.
142.whyCorrect: Judges decide legal disputes and criminal cases independently and solely according to the law.
142.background: According to Article 97 of the Basic Law, judges are independent and subject only to the law. Nobody – not even a government – may tell them how to decide. They hear both sides, examine evidence and then deliver a judgment. To keep them independent, they generally cannot be dismissed or transferred against their will.
142.otherOptions: Citizens are represented in court by lawyers. Parliament changes laws. Young people in court are supported by the youth court assistance service of the youth welfare office.

143.summary: A judge belongs to the judiciary (Judikative).
143.whyCorrect: Judiciary is the technical term for the judicial power.
143.background: State power in Germany is divided into three branches. The judiciary – from the Latin “iudicare”, to judge – consists of the courts and their judges. Article 92 of the Basic Law states: “The judicial power shall be vested in the judges.” The judiciary also checks the other powers: courts can overturn decisions by authorities, and the Federal Constitutional Court can declare laws void.
143.otherOptions: The executive includes the government and administration, the legislature the parliaments. There is no state power called “operative”.

144.summary: A judge belongs to the judicial power (rechtsprechende Gewalt).
144.whyCorrect: This is the German term for the judiciary – the power that administers justice.
144.background: This question asks the same as question 143, just with German instead of Latin terms. The three powers in German are: legislative power (gesetzgebende Gewalt), executive power (vollziehende Gewalt) and judicial power (rechtsprechende Gewalt). This is also how Article 20(3) of the Basic Law puts it. Judicial power is vested in the judges (Article 92).
144.otherOptions: Executive power is the executive (government and administration), legislative power the legislature (parliaments). There is no “planning power”.

145.summary: A judge works for the judiciary.
145.whyCorrect: The judiciary is the judicial power, i.e. the courts.
145.background: The separation of state power is a basic principle of democracy. If the same body could make, implement and judge laws, it would be too powerful. That is why the courts are separate from and independent of parliament and the government. This allows citizens to defend themselves in court even against the state – guaranteed by Article 19(4) of the Basic Law.
145.otherOptions: The executive carries out laws, the legislature passes them. The press is not a state power but independent of the state – even if it is sometimes called the “fourth estate”.
145.memoryTip: Questions 143, 144, 145 and 147: judge = judiciary = administering justice.

146.summary: Proceedings before a court are called a trial (Prozess).
146.whyCorrect: One speaks, for example, of a criminal trial or a civil trial.
146.background: A trial is the regulated procedure in which a court examines and decides a case. In a criminal trial, the question is whether someone has committed a crime. In a civil trial, citizens or companies are in dispute with each other, for example about money or contracts. How a trial works is set out in laws such as the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Code of Civil Procedure. Most hearings are public – you may attend as a spectator.
146.otherOptions: A record (Protokoll) is the written account of what happens in a hearing. “Procedure” (Prozedur) is a general word for a process, and a programme is, for example, a plan or software – none of these is the technical term.

147.summary: A judge’s work is to administer justice (Recht sprechen).
147.whyCorrect: In court proceedings, judges decide what is lawful under the law.
147.background: “Administering justice” means deciding in a specific case what applies under the law – for example, whether a dismissal was valid, who has to pay compensation after an accident or whether a defendant is guilty. Judgments are delivered “in the name of the people”. Many judgments can be appealed so that a higher court reviews the case again.
147.otherOptions: Germany is governed by the federal government, and laws are enacted by parliament. “Drawing up plans” is not a particular task of judges but, for example, of administrations.
147.memoryTip: Judge → administering justice → judgment “in the name of the people”.

148.summary: One of the police’s tasks is to monitor compliance with the law.
148.whyCorrect: The police avert danger and prosecute crimes.
148.background: The police ensure public safety and order. They help in emergencies (emergency number 110), direct traffic, take criminal complaints and investigate crimes on behalf of the public prosecutor’s office. In Germany, policing is mainly the responsibility of the federal states. In addition, there is the Federal Police, which protects borders, railway stations and airports, for example, and the Federal Criminal Police Office. The police are also bound by the law and may only act if a law allows it.
148.otherOptions: Defending the country is the task of the Bundeswehr. Wiretapping citizens is generally forbidden; surveillance is only permitted in narrow exceptions and usually only with a judge’s authorisation. Laws are passed by parliaments.
148.memoryTip: Police = internal security; Bundeswehr = external defence.

149.summary: Denying the Holocaust is an example of antisemitic behaviour.
149.whyCorrect: Holocaust denial is directed against Jews and is a criminal offence in Germany.
149.background: Antisemitism is hostility or hatred towards Jews. Anyone who denies the Holocaust – the murder of around six million European Jews by the National Socialists – mocks the victims and spreads antisemitic conspiracy narratives. In Germany this is punishable as incitement to hatred (Section 130 of the Criminal Code). Other examples of antisemitism are attacks on synagogues, insults against Jews or the claim that Jews control the world.
149.otherOptions: Visiting a Jewish festival shows interest and respect. Criticising the Israeli government is allowed – as with any government; it only becomes antisemitic when Jews as a whole are blamed or Israel’s right to exist is denied. Playing football against a Jewish club is completely normal sport.
149.memoryTip: Denying the Holocaust = antisemitism and a crime.

150.summary: A lay judge (Gerichtsschöffe) is a volunteer judge.
150.whyCorrect: Lay judges take part in criminal proceedings alongside professional judges and have the same voting rights.
150.background: There are around 60,000 lay judges in Germany. They sit, for example, alongside one professional judge at the local court or two or three professional judges at the regional court and help decide on guilt and punishment. They do not need a law degree – on the contrary, their life experience as “ordinary” citizens is what is wanted. The office is voluntary; you can only refuse it for important reasons. This question is closely related to question 140.
150.otherOptions: The deputy of the head of a town is the second mayor or a deputy. Members of the municipal council are elected local politicians. Someone who has studied law is a lawyer – lay judges are precisely non-lawyers.
150.memoryTip: Lay judge = volunteer judge, not a lawyer.

151.summary: The Berlin Wall was built by the GDR.
151.whyCorrect: The GDR leadership had the wall built on 13 August 1961 to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West.
151.background: Until 1961, millions of people fled from the GDR to the Federal Republic, many via West Berlin. To stop this, the SED leadership under Walter Ulbricht sealed off the sector border on the night of 12–13 August 1961. This became a border installation around West Berlin about 155 kilometres long. At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall. On 9 November 1989, the wall opened after peaceful protests by GDR citizens.
151.otherOptions: Britain, the USA and the Federal Republic did not build the wall – West Berlin was on the side that was walled in. The GDR officially called the wall an “anti-fascist protection rampart”; in reality it was meant to stop its own citizens from leaving.
151.memoryTip: Wall: built by the GDR in 1961, fell in 1989.

152.summary: The National Socialists under Adolf Hitler were in power from 1933 to 1945.
152.whyCorrect: Nazi rule began with Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor in 1933 and ended with the surrender in 1945.
152.background: On 30 January 1933, Reich President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler Reich Chancellor. Within a few months the National Socialists built a dictatorship: fundamental rights were suspended, other parties banned and opponents arrested. This was followed by the persecution and murder of Europe’s Jews, the Second World War and millions of deaths. Nazi rule ended with the unconditional surrender on 8 May 1945.
152.otherOptions: 1918 to 1923 was the early period of the Weimar Republic; Hitler failed with a coup attempt in 1923. 1932 to 1950 is wrong, because the National Socialists only came to power in 1933 and were defeated in 1945. 1945 to 1989 was the period of German division.
152.memoryTip: Twelve years of Nazi dictatorship: 1933 to 1945.

153.summary: On 8 May 1945, the Second World War ended in Europe.
153.whyCorrect: On that day the unconditional surrender of the German armed forces took effect.
153.background: With the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht, the fighting in Europe and the Nazi dictatorship ended on 8 May 1945. For many people – concentration camp survivors, forced labourers, the persecuted – it was a day of liberation. In a famous speech in 1985, Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker called 8 May a “day of liberation” from National Socialist tyranny. In Asia, the war continued until Japan’s surrender in September 1945.
153.otherOptions: Hitler had already taken his own life on 30 April 1945. Construction of the Berlin Wall began on 13 August 1961. Konrad Adenauer was elected the first Federal Chancellor in September 1949.
153.memoryTip: 8 May 1945 = end of the war in Europe, “day of liberation”.

154.summary: The Second World War ended in 1945.
154.whyCorrect: In Europe it ended on 8 May 1945, in Asia with Japan’s surrender on 2 September 1945.
154.background: The Second World War began on 1 September 1939 with the German invasion of Poland. It was the most devastating war in history: more than 60 million people died, including the six million murdered Jews. After its defeat, Germany was occupied by the four victorious powers and divided into occupation zones.
154.otherOptions: 1933 was when the National Socialists came to power. In 1949 the Federal Republic and the GDR were founded. In 1961 the Berlin Wall was built. These dates come up often in the test – it is worth knowing them.
154.memoryTip: 1939 war begins – 1945 war ends – 1949 Federal Republic founded.

155.summary: The National Socialists were in power in Germany from 1933 to 1945.
155.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 152, just with different years as answer options.
155.background: After Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor on 30 January 1933, everything happened very quickly: the “Reichstag Fire Decree” in February suspended fundamental rights, and the “Enabling Act” in March allowed the government to pass laws without parliament. By summer 1933, all other parties had been banned or dissolved. This experience still shapes the Basic Law today, for example through the idea of a “defensive democracy”.
155.otherOptions: From 1888 to 1918, Emperor Wilhelm II ruled the German Empire. 1921 to 1934 and 1949 to 1963 do not fit: from 1949 to 1963 Konrad Adenauer was Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic.

156.whyCorrect: Reich President Paul von Hindenburg appointed him on 30 January 1933.
156.background: During the Great Depression from 1929, unemployment and hardship in Germany became very severe, and radical parties gained votes. In the Reichstag election of July 1932, the NSDAP became the strongest party, but it never won a majority of its own in free elections. Conservative politicians believed they could “contain” and control Hitler and persuaded Hindenburg to appoint him Chancellor. This was a grave mistake: within a few months Hitler established a dictatorship.
156.otherOptions: In 1923 Hitler attempted a coup in Munich, which failed. In 1927 he was still far from power. In 1936 the Olympic Games took place in Berlin – by then Hitler had already been in power for three years.

157.summary: In 1933, the National Socialists established a dictatorship.
157.whyCorrect: They abolished fundamental rights, free elections and other parties and ruled through terror.
157.background: Shortly after Hitler took power, Weimar democracy was destroyed. The “Enabling Act” of March 1933 gave the government the right to pass laws without the Reichstag. Trade unions were crushed, parties banned and newspapers brought into line. Political opponents were sent to concentration camps. From 1934, Hitler combined the offices of Reich Chancellor and Reich President as “Führer”.
157.otherOptions: Germany had been a democratic state before, in the Weimar Republic – the National Socialists abolished it. There was no monarchy or principality with a king or prince; the monarchy had ended in 1918.
157.memoryTip: Nazi state = dictatorship: one leader, one party, no freedom.

158.whyCorrect: This is what the National Socialists called their state from 1933 to 1945.
158.background: The term “Third Reich” was a Nazi propaganda term. It was meant to link to the medieval Holy Roman Empire (“First Reich”) and the German Empire of 1871 (“Second Reich”) and to suggest greatness. In reality, the Nazi regime was a dictatorship that persecuted and murdered millions of people and started a world war. Today people usually speak of the “Nazi era” or “Nazi dictatorship”.
158.otherOptions: Democracy came first with the Weimar Republic and then again with the Federal Republic. The German Empire until 1918 was a monarchy. A council republic existed briefly in 1919, for example in Munich.

159.summary: There were no free elections during the National Socialist era.
159.whyCorrect: There was only one party left, the NSDAP; elections and votes were not free.
159.background: After 1933, “elections” to the Reichstag and referendums were still held, but only the NSDAP was left, with a single list, and people were put under pressure. There was no real choice. The Reichstag was meaningless and merely approved. That is why the Basic Law today specially protects the electoral principles and the diversity of parties.
159.otherOptions: Press censorship, arbitrary arrests and the persecution of Jews very much existed in the Nazi state – they were typical of the dictatorship. The question asks what did not exist.
159.memoryTip: Watch for “not”: the Nazi state had no free elections.

160.summary: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945.
160.whyCorrect: It began with the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939.
160.background: The Second World War was started by Nazi Germany. German troops occupied large parts of Europe; in the east, the Wehrmacht waged a war of annihilation. More than 60 million people died – soldiers and above all civilians. In the shadow of the war, the National Socialists murdered around six million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma. The war ended in Europe on 8 May 1945.
160.otherOptions: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918. The Vietnam War took place mainly in the 1960s and 1970s, and the Gulf War in 1990/91 in the Persian Gulf.
160.memoryTip: First World War 1914–1918, Second World War 1939–1945.

161.summary: The Nazi state was characterised by a policy of state racism.
161.whyCorrect: The National Socialists divided people into “races” and persecuted and murdered millions who did not fit their worldview.
161.background: Racism was at the core of Nazi ideology. With the “Nuremberg Laws” of 1935, the National Socialists stripped Jews of their civil rights and banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews. Deportations and the Holocaust followed. Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities, homosexuals and many others were also persecuted and murdered. That is why the Basic Law places human dignity and the prohibition of discrimination at its very beginning.
161.otherOptions: Freedom of expression, freedom of religion and democracy did not exist in the Nazi state – they were precisely what was abolished. Today these rights are guaranteed in the Basic Law.
161.memoryTip: Nazi state = racism, persecution, no freedom.

162.summary: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg became known for the assassination attempt on Hitler on 20 July 1944.
162.whyCorrect: The officer planted a bomb at Hitler’s headquarters; Hitler survived, and Stauffenberg was shot that same night.
162.background: Stauffenberg was a Wehrmacht officer and belonged to a resistance group that wanted to kill Hitler and end the war. On 20 July 1944 he brought a bomb into the “Wolf’s Lair” in East Prussia. Hitler was only slightly injured. Stauffenberg and other conspirators were shot that same evening at the Bendlerblock in Berlin, and many others were executed later. Today the German Resistance Memorial Center there commemorates all those who opposed the Nazi regime.
162.otherOptions: Gold medals in 1936 were won by athletes such as Jesse Owens. The Reichstag building was built at the end of the 19th century. The Wehrmacht was built up by the National Socialists from 1935 – Stauffenberg turned against its leadership.

163.summary: In 1938 the National Socialists destroyed synagogues and Jewish shops in Germany.
163.whyCorrect: The November pogroms took place on the night of 9–10 November 1938.
163.background: During the pogrom night, the SA, SS and other Nazi supporters destroyed more than 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms throughout Germany, as well as thousands of Jewish shops and homes. Hundreds of people were killed and around 30,000 Jewish men were taken to concentration camps. The National Socialists played the night down as “Kristallnacht” (Night of Broken Glass). The pogroms were a step from exclusion towards the annihilation of the Jews.
163.otherOptions: In 1925 and 1930 the National Socialists were not yet in power. In 1945, Nazi rule ended with the end of the war.

164.summary: On 9 November 1938, National Socialists and their supporters destroyed Jewish shops and synagogues.
164.whyCorrect: These were the November pogroms, often called the “pogrom night”.
164.background: The violence was orchestrated by the Nazi leadership and presented as “spontaneous popular anger”. The police and fire brigades did not intervene to protect Jews. Afterwards, the victims were even made to pay for the damage themselves. 9 November is a special day in German history: in 1918 the republic was proclaimed, in 1923 Hitler’s coup failed, in 1938 the synagogues burned and in 1989 the Berlin Wall fell.
164.otherOptions: The Second World War only began on 1 September 1939 with the attack on Poland. The National Socialists did not lose an election in 1938 – there were no free elections any more. Hitler made himself head of state in 1934 after Hindenburg’s death; he had already banned the parties in 1933.
164.memoryTip: 9 November: 1918 republic, 1938 pogrom, 1989 fall of the Wall.

165.summary: The first Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany was Konrad Adenauer.
165.whyCorrect: Konrad Adenauer (CDU) was Federal Chancellor from 1949 to 1963.
165.background: Before 1933, Konrad Adenauer was Lord Mayor of Cologne and was removed from office by the National Socialists. In 1949, the first Bundestag elected him Chancellor with a majority of just one vote. During his time in office he firmly anchored the Federal Republic in the West: Germany joined NATO, co-founded the European Communities and was reconciled with France. When he resigned in 1963 he was 87 years old.
165.otherOptions: Kurt Georg Kiesinger (CDU) was Chancellor from 1966 to 1969, Willy Brandt (SPD) from 1969 to 1974 and Helmut Schmidt (SPD) from 1974 to 1982 – all after Adenauer.

166.summary: People chanted “We are the people” at the Monday demonstrations in the GDR in 1989.
166.whyCorrect: With this chant, GDR citizens peacefully demanded freedom and democracy from the SED leadership.
166.background: In autumn 1989, thousands of people took to the streets every Monday, especially in Leipzig, after the prayers for peace at St Nicholas Church. On 9 October 1989, there were around 70,000 – and despite fears of violence, the security forces did not intervene. The chant “We are the people” meant: not the party, but the people should decide. Later it became “We are one people” – the wish for reunification. On 9 November 1989 the Wall fell.
166.otherOptions: The workers’ uprising of 17 June 1953 in the GDR was crushed by Soviet tanks. In 1968, mainly students protested in the Federal Republic. The anti-nuclear movement demonstrated against nuclear power plants in the 1970s and 1980s.
166.memoryTip: Leipzig 1989, Monday demonstrations: “We are the people”.

167.summary: The Allied occupying powers were the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France.
167.whyCorrect: After the victory over Nazi Germany, these four states divided Germany into four occupation zones.
167.background: At the Yalta Conference (February 1945) and in Potsdam (summer 1945), the victorious powers decided how they would administer Germany. Each of the four powers received a zone; Berlin was also divided into four sectors. Together they formed the Allied Control Council. The Federal Republic emerged from the three western zones in 1949, the GDR from the Soviet zone. Only with the Two Plus Four Treaty in 1990 did united Germany regain full sovereignty.
167.otherOptions: Italy and Japan were Nazi Germany’s allies in the war; Sweden, Spain and Portugal remained neutral. Poland was one of the victims of the German attack but was not an occupying power in Germany.
167.memoryTip: Four powers: USA, Soviet Union, Great Britain, France.

168.summary: Japan was not an Allied occupying power in Germany.
168.whyCorrect: Japan fought on the side of Nazi Germany in the Second World War and was among the defeated.
168.background: In the Second World War, two camps faced each other: the “Axis powers” with Germany, Italy and Japan, and the Allies including the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France. After the war, the four Allied powers occupied Germany. Japan itself was occupied, mainly by the USA. It surrendered in September 1945 after the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
168.otherOptions: The USA, the Soviet Union and France were – together with Great Britain – the four occupying powers in Germany.
168.memoryTip: Japan = Germany’s ally in the war, not an occupying power.

169.summary: The Federal Republic of Germany was founded in 1949.
169.whyCorrect: The Federal Republic came into being when the Basic Law entered into force in May 1949.
169.background: After the war, the three Western powers allowed the states in their zones to draft a constitution. The Parliamentary Council in Bonn wrote the Basic Law, which was promulgated on 23 May 1949. The first Bundestag was elected in August 1949, and Konrad Adenauer became Chancellor in September. Bonn became the provisional capital. In October 1949 the GDR was founded in the Soviet zone – Germany was now divided for 40 years.
169.otherOptions: The Second World War began in 1939 and ended in 1945. In 1951, among other things, the Federal Constitutional Court was established and the Federal Republic signed the treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community.
169.memoryTip: 1949: Basic Law, Federal Republic, GDR – all in one year.

170.summary: During the National Socialist era, parties were banned.
170.whyCorrect: By July 1933, all parties except the NSDAP had been banned or forced to dissolve.
170.background: After taking power, the National Socialists first banned the KPD and then the SPD. The other parties dissolved themselves under pressure. In July 1933, a law declared the NSDAP the only party in Germany. Germany was thus a one-party state. That is why the Basic Law today guarantees the freedom to found parties (Article 21), and only the Federal Constitutional Court may ban a party.
170.otherOptions: The free development of one’s personality, freedom of the press and the protection of human dignity did not exist in the Nazi state. They are fundamental rights that were only guaranteed by the Basic Law in 1949 (Articles 1, 2 and 5).
170.memoryTip: Nazi state: one party – all others banned.

171.summary: Social market economy means: the economy follows supply and demand, but the state ensures social balance.
171.whyCorrect: It combines the freedom of the market with social security.
171.background: In the social market economy, companies and consumers decide freely what is produced and bought; prices are formed on the market. But the state steps in where the market alone would be unfair: it protects employees, provides social insurance, pays assistance to those in need, sets a minimum wage and prevents monopolies through competition law. This model was shaped by Ludwig Erhard after 1948 and is considered the basis of the “economic miracle”. See also question 50.
171.otherOptions: An economy guided solely by supply and demand would be a pure (free) market economy without social balance. An economy planned by the state is a planned economy, as in the GDR. Foreign demand is important for exports but does not determine the economic system.

172.summary: The GDR was founded in the Soviet occupation zone.
172.whyCorrect: The German Democratic Republic was established there on 7 October 1949.
172.background: After 1945, the Soviet Union occupied the eastern part of Germany. There, together with the SED, it built a socialist system on the Soviet model. The GDR was founded in October 1949, a few months after the Federal Republic. The GDR was a dictatorship of the SED, with a planned economy, the state security service (Stasi) and no free elections. It existed until reunification on 3 October 1990.
172.otherOptions: The Federal Republic of Germany emerged from the American, British and French zones in 1949.

173.summary: The Federal Republic of Germany is a founding member of the European Union.
173.whyCorrect: In 1951 and 1957 it was one of the six founding states of the European Communities, from which the EU developed.
173.background: After the war, former enemies wanted to secure peace through cooperation. In 1951, Belgium, the Federal Republic, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands founded the European Coal and Steel Community. In 1957, the Treaties of Rome created the European Economic Community and Euratom. These became the European Union in 1993 with the Maastricht Treaty. Today the EU has 27 member states.
173.otherOptions: NATO was founded in 1949 without Germany; the Federal Republic joined in 1955. Both German states only joined the United Nations in 1973. The GDR belonged to the Warsaw Pact, not the Federal Republic.
173.memoryTip: Founding member = there from the start: the EU (or its predecessors).

174.whyCorrect: The German Democratic Republic was established on 7 October 1949 in the Soviet occupation zone.
174.background: 1949 was the year two German states were founded: in May the Federal Republic came into being with the Basic Law, in October the GDR. The GDR existed for about 41 years. After the Peaceful Revolution of 1989 and the first free elections to the People’s Chamber in March 1990, it joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. That day is now a national holiday, the Day of German Unity.
174.otherOptions: In 1947 there were no German states yet, only occupation zones. On 17 June 1953 there was the popular uprising in the GDR. In 1956 the GDR founded its army, the National People’s Army.
174.memoryTip: 1949: two German states – Federal Republic (May) and GDR (October).

175.summary: After the Second World War there were four occupation zones in Germany.
175.whyCorrect: The USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France each administered one zone.
175.background: The American zone lay mainly in the south (including Bavaria and Hesse), the British zone in the north-west, the French zone in the south-west and the Soviet zone in the east. Berlin lay in the middle of the Soviet zone but was also divided into four sectors. When the Soviet Union blocked access routes to West Berlin in 1948/49, the Western Allies supplied the city for almost a year via an airlift.
175.otherOptions: Three, five or six zones are wrong – there were exactly four occupying powers and therefore four zones. France only received its zone later, created from parts of the American and British zones.

176.summary: The zones were distributed as follows: 1 = Great Britain, 2 = Soviet Union, 3 = USA, 4 = France.
176.whyCorrect: The British occupied the north-west, the Soviets the east, the Americans the south and the French the south-west.
176.background: On the map, zone 1 in the north-west is the British zone, including today’s North Rhine-Westphalia, Lower Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg. Zone 2 in the east is the Soviet zone, which later became the GDR. Zone 3 in the south is the American zone with Bavaria and Hesse; Bremen also belonged to it so that the USA had its own port. Zone 4 in the south-west is the French zone, including today’s Rhineland-Palatinate.
176.otherOptions: The other answers mix up the powers. Geography helps: the Soviet Union lay to the east, so it occupied the east; France borders Germany in the south-west; Britain lies across the North Sea to the north-west.
176.memoryTip: Geography helps: British in the north, Soviets in the east, Americans in the south, French in the south-west.

177.summary: Berlin was divided into four sectors after the Second World War.
177.whyCorrect: Like Germany as a whole, the capital was divided between the four victorious powers.
177.background: Although Berlin lay in the middle of the Soviet zone, each victorious power received a sector of the city. The Soviet sector in the east became East Berlin, the capital of the GDR. The American, British and French sectors formed West Berlin, which was closely tied to the Federal Republic. From 1961, the Wall separated the two parts. A well-known symbol of this period is “Checkpoint Charlie”, a crossing point between the American and Soviet sectors.
177.otherOptions: Munich was in the American zone, Dresden and Frankfurt (Oder) in the Soviet zone. These cities were not divided into sectors.
177.memoryTip: Four powers, four sectors – only in Berlin.

178.summary: The airlift was necessary because the Soviet Union cut off all land traffic to West Berlin.
178.whyCorrect: With the Berlin Blockade, the Soviet Union wanted to force the Western powers out of Berlin.
178.background: In June 1948 the Western powers introduced the Deutsche Mark in their zones. The Soviet Union responded with a blockade: roads, railways and waterways to West Berlin were closed. American and British aircraft in particular then supplied the roughly two million West Berliners from the air for almost a year – with food, coal and medicine. Berliners called the planes “raisin bombers”. In May 1949 the Soviet Union lifted the blockade.
178.otherOptions: The airlift was neither cheaper nor faster than land transport – it was much more expensive and complex. It was necessary because there was no other way, not because of fear of attacks.
178.memoryTip: Blockade on the ground → bridge in the air.

179.summary: The Second World War officially ended in Europe with Germany’s unconditional surrender.
