179.whyCorrect: The surrender of the German armed forces took effect on 8 May 1945.
179.background: The German armed forces signed the unconditional surrender on 7 May 1945 in Reims and again on the night of 8–9 May in Berlin-Karlshorst. “Unconditional” meant that Germany could set no conditions, and the victorious powers took over supreme governmental authority. This ended the fighting in Europe. Today the Berlin-Karlshorst Museum, among others, commemorates this moment.
179.otherOptions: Hitler had already taken his own life on 30 April 1945, but the war continued for more than a week afterwards. There was no orderly withdrawal from the occupied territories. A revolution ended the First World War in 1918 (the November Revolution), not the Second.

180.summary: The first Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic was Konrad Adenauer.
180.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 165: Adenauer (CDU) governed from 1949 to 1963.
180.background: Konrad Adenauer shaped the early years of the Federal Republic so strongly that people speak of the “Adenauer era”. In 1955 he travelled to Moscow and secured the release of the last roughly 10,000 German prisoners of war. In 1963 he concluded the Élysée Treaty with French President Charles de Gaulle, the foundation of Franco-German friendship.
180.otherOptions: Ludwig Erhard was Adenauer’s economics minister and succeeded him in 1963 as the second Federal Chancellor. Willy Brandt (1969–1974) and Gerhard Schröder (1998–2005) were later SPD chancellors.

181.summary: With his genuflection, Willy Brandt asked Poland and the Polish Jews for forgiveness.
181.whyCorrect: Kneeling before the memorial to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto was a gesture of humility and a plea for reconciliation.
181.background: On 7 December 1970, Federal Chancellor Willy Brandt was in Warsaw to sign the Treaty of Warsaw, in which the Federal Republic recognised the border with Poland. At the memorial to the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising he laid a wreath – and then unexpectedly knelt down. Without words, he expressed shame for the German crimes. The photo went around the world. In 1971 Brandt received the Nobel Peace Prize for his policy of reconciliation with the East.
181.otherOptions: Brandt did not submit to the Allies and did not show humility towards the Warsaw Pact, the Eastern military alliance. He did also visit the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, but the famous genuflection took place at the Ghetto memorial.

182.summary: The Jewish house of prayer is called a synagogue.
182.whyCorrect: The Jewish community gathers in the synagogue to pray, read the Torah and learn.
182.background: The word synagogue comes from Greek and means “assembly”. The most important service takes place on the Sabbath, which begins on Friday evening. At its centre is the Torah, which is kept on scrolls in the Torah ark. The community is often led by a rabbi. Many synagogues in Germany are under police protection today because antisemitic attacks keep happening.
182.otherOptions: A church is the Christian house of worship; a basilica is a particular architectural style or an honorary title for certain churches. A mosque is the house of prayer of Muslims.
182.memoryTip: Church – Christians, mosque – Muslims, synagogue – Jews.

183.summary: The “economic miracle” in the Federal Republic took place in the 1950s.
183.whyCorrect: After the currency reform of 1948, the West German economy grew exceptionally fast in the 1950s.
183.background: After the war, many cities lay in ruins. With the introduction of the Deutsche Mark in 1948, aid from the American Marshall Plan and the social market economy under economics minister Ludwig Erhard, a rapid upswing began. Production rose, unemployment fell almost to zero and many families could afford a fridge, television or car for the first time. Because there was a labour shortage, the Federal Republic concluded recruitment agreements with other countries from 1955, including Turkey in 1961.
183.otherOptions: The 1940s were marked by war and post-war hardship. In the 1970s the oil crisis of 1973 brought economic problems, and in the 1980s unemployment was comparatively high.
183.memoryTip: Economic miracle = 1950s, Deutsche Mark, Ludwig Erhard.

184.summary: The State of Israel was founded on the basis of a United Nations resolution.
184.whyCorrect: In November 1947, the UN General Assembly adopted a partition plan for Palestine.
184.background: On 29 November 1947, the United Nations General Assembly voted in Resolution 181 to divide what was then the British Mandate of Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state. On 14 May 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel. For many Holocaust survivors, Israel became a new home. The Federal Republic and Israel established diplomatic relations in 1965.
184.otherOptions: The Zionist Congress of 1897 in Basel under Theodor Herzl formulated the goal of a Jewish homeland, but was not a legal basis for founding the state. There was no federal government in 1947. The Soviet Union recognised Israel early on but did not propose its founding.

185.summary: The “Iron Curtain” stood for the Warsaw Pact sealing itself off from the West.
185.whyCorrect: It referred to the guarded border that divided Europe into East and West during the Cold War.
185.background: The term was popularised by the British politician Winston Churchill in 1946. He used it to describe how the Soviet Union and the Eastern European states it controlled sealed themselves off from the West. The Iron Curtain ran from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea – right through Germany, where the inner-German border was secured with fences, mines and watchtowers. It fell in 1989, when Hungary opened its border and the Wall fell in the GDR.
185.otherOptions: There was never such a border between northern and southern Germany. The term has nothing to do with Nazi Germany against the Allies, and Europe was not sealed off from the USA – Western Europe and the USA were allies in the Cold War.
185.memoryTip: Iron Curtain = the border between East and West in the Cold War.

186.summary: The uprising in the GDR took place on 17 June 1953.
186.whyCorrect: In the Federal Republic, 17 June was a public holiday called the “Day of German Unity” until 1990.
186.background: On 16 and 17 June 1953, construction workers in East Berlin first protested against higher work quotas. This quickly became an uprising across the whole GDR, in which hundreds of thousands demanded free elections and the government’s resignation. Soviet tanks crushed the uprising; dozens of people were killed and thousands arrested. Since reunification, 3 October has been the Day of German Unity; in Berlin, the “Straße des 17. Juni” commemorates 17 June.
186.otherOptions: 1 May is Labour Day. The assassination attempt on Hitler took place on 20 July 1944. 9 November is the day the Wall fell in 1989 and of the pogroms in 1938.
186.memoryTip: 17 June 1953 – popular uprising in the GDR.

187.summary: The black, red and gold flag with hammer, compass and wreath of grain was the flag of the GDR.
187.whyCorrect: From 1959, the GDR flag bore the GDR’s state emblem in the centre.
187.background: The Federal Republic and the GDR both used the colours black, red and gold, which go back to the democratic movement of the 19th century. To distinguish itself, the GDR placed its emblem in the centre in 1959: the hammer stood for the workers, the compass for the intelligentsia and the wreath of grain for the farmers. This flag disappeared with reunification in 1990.
187.otherOptions: Prussia had a black and white flag. The flag of the Federal Republic is black, red and gold without a symbol. The “Third Reich” used the swastika flag.
187.memoryTip: Hammer + compass + grain = workers, intelligentsia, farmers = GDR.

188.summary: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961.
188.whyCorrect: On 13 August 1961, the GDR began sealing off the border with West Berlin.
188.background: Only two months earlier, GDR leader Walter Ulbricht had said at a press conference: “Nobody intends to build a wall.” On the night of 12–13 August 1961, soldiers and police first closed the border with barbed wire, and then the Wall was built. Families and friends were separated overnight. The Wall stood for 28 years, until 9 November 1989.
188.otherOptions: 1953 was the year of the popular uprising in the GDR. 1956 and 1959 are not significant years for the Wall.
188.memoryTip: Wall built 13 August 1961 – Wall fell 9 November 1989.

189.summary: The GDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
189.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 188, just with different years.
189.background: The reason for building the Wall was mass emigration: between 1949 and 1961, around three million people had left the GDR, mainly young and well-educated people. The GDR was at risk of running out of workers. After the Wall was built, escaping was life-threatening: there was a shoot-to-kill order at the border. Nevertheless, many tried – through tunnels, by balloon or across the Baltic Sea.
189.otherOptions: In 1919 the Weimar Constitution was adopted, in 1933 the National Socialists came to power, and in 1990 Germany was reunified – by then the Wall had already fallen.

190.summary: GDR stands for German Democratic Republic (Deutsche Demokratische Republik, DDR).
190.whyCorrect: This was the name of the East German state from 1949 to 1990.
190.background: Although “democratic” was in its name, the GDR was not a democracy. The Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED) controlled all areas of the state. Elections had only a single list, the press was censored and the state security service monitored the population. Anyone who criticised the system risked prison. Only the Peaceful Revolution of 1989 brought free elections.
190.otherOptions: “Third German Broadcasting”, “The German Republic” and “Third German Republic” are invented names.
190.memoryTip: D-D-R: Deutsche (German) – Demokratische (Democratic) – Republik (Republic) – but not a democracy.

191.summary: The Berlin Wall was opened to everyone in 1989.
191.whyCorrect: On the evening of 9 November 1989, the border crossings opened and thousands of East Berliners streamed into the West.
191.background: After mass protests and a wave of emigration via Hungary, the GDR leadership wanted to relax travel rules. At a press conference on 9 November 1989, SED politician Günter Schabowski was asked when this would apply and answered: “As far as I know … immediately, without delay.” That same evening thousands of people crowded the border crossings until the guards opened them. The images of jubilant people on the Wall went around the world.
191.otherOptions: In 1987, US President Ronald Reagan demanded in Berlin: “Tear down this wall!” – but the Wall was still standing. 1992 and 1995 were already after reunification in 1990.

192.summary: Brandenburg used to be part of the GDR.
192.whyCorrect: Brandenburg is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
192.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Brandenburg is Potsdam. Brandenburg surrounds Berlin; Sanssouci Palace is in Potsdam.
192.otherOptions: Bavaria, Saarland and Hesse were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
192.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

193.summary: From 1961 to 1989, Berlin was divided by a wall.
193.whyCorrect: The Wall separated East Berlin, the capital of the GDR, from West Berlin.
193.background: For 28 years the Wall ran right through the city and around West Berlin. It cut through streets, squares and even cemeteries. West Berliners could only travel to the East with special permits, and East Berliners were usually not allowed to go to the West at all. Today the Berlin Wall Memorial on Bernauer Straße, the East Side Gallery and a double row of cobblestones in the ground mark where the Wall ran.
193.otherOptions: Berlin always had mayors – in the West the Governing Mayor, in the East a Lord Mayor. West Berlin was not a separate state but closely tied to the Federal Republic. And West Berlin was not only reachable by plane: there were transit roads and rail connections through the GDR.

194.summary: On 3 October, Germany celebrates the Day of German Unity.
194.whyCorrect: On this day in 1990, the GDR joined the Federal Republic – Germany was reunified.
194.background: The Day of German Unity is Germany’s national holiday and a public holiday in all federal states. It commemorates reunification on 3 October 1990, made possible by the Peaceful Revolution in the GDR and the Two Plus Four Treaty with the four victorious powers. The main celebration takes place in a different state each year, usually the one currently chairing the Bundesrat.
194.otherOptions: There is no “Day of the Nation”, “Day of the Federal States” or “Day of the Cities” as a public holiday.

195.summary: Saxony-Anhalt used to be part of the GDR.
195.whyCorrect: Saxony-Anhalt is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
195.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Saxony-Anhalt is Magdeburg. In Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Luther published his theses in 1517 – the start of the Reformation.
195.otherOptions: Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Saarland were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
195.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

196.summary: The period in autumn 1989 is called “Die Wende” (the turning point) because the GDR changed from a dictatorship to a democracy.
196.whyCorrect: Through peaceful protests the SED lost its power; in 1990 the first free elections were held in the GDR.
196.background: In autumn 1989, hundreds of thousands demonstrated in the GDR for freedom, freedom to travel and democracy, while many fled to the West via Hungary and Czechoslovakia. In October, head of state Erich Honecker had to resign, and in November the Wall fell. On 18 March 1990, the first free elections to the People’s Chamber took place. Because everything happened without violence, it is often called the “Peaceful Revolution” today.
196.otherOptions: The GDR had not been a liberal market economy before, but socialist with a planned economy. It was never a monarchy, nor a religious state – on the contrary, religion was pushed back in the GDR.

197.summary: Thuringia used to be part of the GDR.
197.whyCorrect: Thuringia is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
197.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Thuringia is Erfurt. Goethe and Schiller lived in Weimar, and in 1919 the National Assembly met there and adopted the Weimar Constitution.
197.otherOptions: Hesse, Bavaria and Bremen were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
197.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

198.summary: Saxony used to be part of the GDR.
198.whyCorrect: Saxony is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
198.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Saxony is Dresden. The Monday demonstrations that helped bring down the Wall began in Leipzig in 1989.
198.otherOptions: Bavaria, Lower Saxony and Baden-Württemberg were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.

200.summary: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania used to be part of the GDR.
200.whyCorrect: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
